subject: ela
cluster: Research to build and present knowledge
skillName: Gather relevant information from multiple sources
description: Students gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources to answer a research question. They judge whether a source is credible (who wrote it, when, why, and how trustworthy the evidence is), select the information that actually answers the question while discarding off-topic detail, and decide when to quote exactly versus paraphrase in their own words. They avoid plagiarism by putting borrowed ideas into their own words or marking direct quotations, and they provide basic bibliographic information (author, title, source or website, and date) so a reader could find the source. Because this is a writing and research standard, every item embeds the full research question, source excerpt, citation, or short passage it depends on inside the item itself, so the student needs nothing external. Items test the components of gathering, evaluating, citing, and avoiding plagiarism through identify, analyze, and evaluate tasks plus short construction, not full research reports.
subSkills: Identify which sources or pieces of information are relevant to a given research question and which are off topic

Assess the credibility of a source using signals such as author expertise, publication date, purpose (to inform versus to sell or persuade), evidence offered, and type of website (for example .gov, .edu, a personal blog, or an ad)
Compare two or more sources and judge which is more credible or more relevant for a specific question
Decide when to quote a source word for word (precise wording matters) and when to paraphrase (restate the idea in your own words)
Paraphrase a sentence or short passage accurately in your own words without changing the meaning
Recognize plagiarism, including copying without quotation marks, swapping a few words while keeping the original sentence structure, and using an idea without crediting the source
Mark a direct quotation correctly with quotation marks and credit the author
Provide and identify basic bibliographic information: author, title, source or website name, and date
Identify what bibliographic element is missing or incorrect in a citation

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the relevant source
problemArchetypes.example: Research question embedded in the item: 'How do honeybees help farmers grow crops?' Four short source titles are listed: A 'Honeybee Pollination and Crop Yields' (a university farming guide), B 'Top Ten Honey Dessert Recipes' (a food blog), C 'The History of Beekeeping Hats' (a hobby site), D 'How to Remove a Wasp Nest' (a pest control ad). Which source is most relevant to the research question? Answer: A, because it directly addresses how bees affect crops, while the others are off topic.

problemArchetypes.name: Assess source credibility
problemArchetypes.example: Research question: 'Is the local river safe to swim in?' Read the two source descriptions in the item. Source 1: a report from the state environmental agency website (.gov), updated this year, citing water test results. Source 2: a comment on a social media post from a user who says 'I think it is fine, I swam once.' Which source is more credible and why? Answer: Source 1, because it comes from an expert agency, is recent, and provides tested evidence rather than one person's opinion.

problemArchetypes.name: Quote or paraphrase decision
problemArchetypes.example: A student is researching weather. Read the source sentence in the item: 'A tornado's wind speed can reach 300 miles per hour.' The student wants to include the exact figure in a report. Should the student quote or paraphrase, and how? Answer: either is acceptable, but if quoting the wording must stay exact and use quotation marks; a correct paraphrase is 'Tornado winds can blow as fast as 300 miles per hour,' which keeps the meaning in the student's own words.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the plagiarized version
problemArchetypes.example: Read the original source sentence embedded in the item: 'Volcanic ash can travel thousands of miles and disrupt air travel.' Four student versions follow. Which one is plagiarism? Answer: the version that copies the sentence almost word for word with no quotation marks and no credit, or the version that only swaps 'travel' for 'move' while keeping the same structure, because changing a few words is still plagiarism.

problemArchetypes.name: Choose the accurate paraphrase
problemArchetypes.example: Read the source sentence in the item: 'Most of the oxygen we breathe is produced by ocean plants, not trees.' Which choice is an accurate paraphrase in the student's own words? Answer: 'Ocean plants, rather than trees, make most of the oxygen people breathe.' Distractors either copy the original wording or change its meaning (for example, claiming trees make the most oxygen).

problemArchetypes.name: Complete or fix the citation
problemArchetypes.example: Read the citation embedded in the item: 'Maria Lopez. "Saving the Coral Reefs." Ocean Today. 2022.' Then a second citation is shown that lists only a title and date. Which bibliographic element is missing from the second citation? Answer: the author and the source or website name, because a basic citation needs author, title, source, and date so a reader can find it.

Easy.description: A single research question plus one short source description, citation, or sentence (roughly 10 to 30 words total) embedded in the item. The task is identify-level: pick the obviously relevant source from clearly off-topic options, name whether a source is credible or not when the signal is unmistakable (a .gov agency report versus an ad), choose the one sentence that is a direct copy, or identify a single missing citation element. Only one component is tested and the correct answer is clear.
constraints: Stimulus is one short source title, a one-sentence source, or a single citation included in the prompt
Tests exactly one component (relevance, an obvious credibility signal, a clear copy, or one missing citation part)
Identify-level task: select or label, no construction required
Distractors are clearly weaker (a topic that is plainly off point or a source that is plainly an ad or a personal opinion)

Medium.description: A research question with two short source descriptions or a 2 to 4 line source passage (roughly 30 to 60 words) embedded in the item. The task is analyze-level: compare two sources and choose the more credible or more relevant one, choose the accurate paraphrase among versions that are partly defensible, identify which student version crosses into plagiarism when one only swaps a few words, or decide whether to quote or paraphrase in a given situation. The student must weigh more than one plausible option.
constraints: Stimulus is two short source descriptions or a brief source passage in the prompt
Tests credibility comparison, accurate paraphrasing, the quote-versus-paraphrase decision, or near-copy plagiarism
Analyze-level task: compare, paraphrase, or judge based on relevance and credibility
Distractors are plausible partial fits (a source that is relevant but less credible, a paraphrase that keeps too much original wording, or a quote with a small error)

Hard.description: A research question with two or three short sources, a multi-sentence source passage, or a passage paired with a student draft (roughly 60 to 110 words) embedded in the item. The task is evaluate-level: judge which combination of sources best and most credibly answers the question, decide why a paraphrase fails (it changed the meaning or stayed too close to the original) and which fixes it, evaluate a short student passage to find the sentence that plagiarizes and explain why, or determine which citation is both complete and correctly formatted. Requires inference about purpose, credibility, and how borrowing was handled across the passage.
constraints: Stimulus is two or three short sources, a multi-sentence passage, or a source plus a student draft included in the prompt
Tests how multiple components interact: relevance, credibility, paraphrase accuracy, plagiarism, and citation
Evaluate-level task: select the best sourcing, the correct fix, or the fully correct citation and justify it
Requires inference to judge a source's purpose, the credibility tradeoff, and whether borrowed material was properly handled

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats any source that mentions the general topic as relevant, ignoring whether it actually answers the research question
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Picks a honey dessert recipe blog as relevant to 'How do honeybees help farmers grow crops?' just because it mentions bees

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student judges credibility by how confident or appealing a source sounds rather than by author expertise, purpose, evidence, and date
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a flashy advertisement or a strongly worded personal blog post over a recent government or university report because it sounds sure of itself

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes anything found online or any website is equally trustworthy and ignores the type of site or its purpose
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Treats an ad selling a product or an anonymous social media comment as just as credible as an expert agency page

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes that changing or swapping a few words makes copied text original, not realizing this is still plagiarism
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Selects a version that keeps the source's exact sentence structure and only replaces one or two words as an acceptable paraphrase

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks copying a sentence exactly is acceptable as long as it is true, without quotation marks or credit to the author
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Marks a word-for-word copy with no quotation marks and no source as a correct, non-plagiarized version

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student paraphrases by changing wording but accidentally changes the meaning of the source
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Chooses a paraphrase that reverses or distorts the idea, such as saying trees make the most oxygen when the source said ocean plants do

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student thinks a citation only needs the title, or only the website, and does not require author and date
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Accepts a citation that lists just a title and date, or just a web address, as complete bibliographic information

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student always quotes directly instead of paraphrasing, or always paraphrases even when exact wording matters, without judging which fits the situation
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Insists on quoting an entire passage when a paraphrase is appropriate, or paraphrases an exact statistic or definition that should be quoted precisely
